name: Olga Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpentry foreman for a contractor that refurbishes social housing, mostly old council blocks from the sixties. My crew of four does the second fix: new doors, kitchens, skirting, stair treads, whatever the flat needs once the walls are back up. Every flat has a tenant still living in it, so half my day is carpentry and half is talking to a grandmother about where her china cabinet goes. I love that part, honestly. What wears me out is walls that aren't straight anywhere and a programme that pretends they are.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, she drives the number 14 bus for the city. We rent, we've got about three months of bills saved, and we're careful but not struggling. I use an AI chat thing now and then to tidy up my snag reports, the lists of small faults at the end of a job, or to translate a note for a tenant who doesn't read English well. I didn't trust it at first, but once a few of the other foremen used it, I gave it a go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pretty much what I say now: the tools are handy for paperwork and that's it. On the crew chat I'd joke that the robot uprising got cancelled. Then I'd go back to arguing with the housing association about budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means not much changes for me, and I'm fine with that. Refurb work in old buildings needs someone who can see that a wall's three centimetres out and fix it so the door still closes. My real worry would just be whether the council keeps funding the refurb programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep running my crew on the Elm Park blocks, which have about two years of flats left. Keep using the chat tool for snag lists, maybe save half an hour a week. And put a bit more into savings, maybe 150 a month, because Ana and I want a few more months behind us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, because all the big talk would turn out to be nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned council funding. How sure are you of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. The programme got cut by a fifth two years ago and we lost a crew. The real threat to my job was never a robot, it was a council spreadsheet with a red line through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be relieved. Her depot keeps putting up posters about driverless trials, and she pretends not to read them. If nothing happens, she gets to stop pretending.

say: I'd say the tools are **handy for paperwork** and little else.
I'd joke that the **robot uprising** got cancelled, then get back to budget fights.
think: Old buildings need someone who can see a wall is **out of true** and fix it.
My real risk stays **council funding** for the refurb programme, not AI.
do: Keep running my crew on the **Elm Park** blocks for about two more years.
Keep using the **chat tool** for snag lists to save time.
Add about **150 a month** to savings with Ana.
feel: **Calm**, and slightly flat that the big talk came to nothing.
S0.quote: The real threat to my job was never a robot, it was a council spreadsheet with a red line through it.
fieldNote: She places her risk in **public budgets**, which fits her progressive outlook.
Her work is hands-on but full of **tenant contact**, which she values most.
Ana's **bus job** quietly shadows her answers even in the mildest picture.

steps.text: Keep running the second-fix crew on the Elm Park blocks
Keep using the chat tool to write snag lists
Add 150 a month to the joint savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when unions and councils need to step up, not wait. Online I'd share stuff about retraining money, because the people losing office jobs at the housing association are my neighbours too. On site I'd say we're fine for a while, which is true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the paperwork side of a foreman's job shrinks, the snag lists, the material orders, the daily reports. That's maybe a fifth of my week. What I'd really think about is Ana, because her depot would push those driverless trials harder, and I don't know if driving counts as thinking or hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the new site software properly instead of dodging it, so I'm the foreman who gets the job done fastest. Join the union, which I keep meaning to do. And Ana and I would sit down and price out what she'd need to retrain if the trials go ahead, maybe as a depot engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job looks okay, but I'd be watching Ana's face every time the news comes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you keep meaning to join the union. Why haven't you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Laziness, honestly, and the fees. Our firm isn't a union shop. In this picture I'd stop putting it off, because a contract that says how the new software gets used is worth more than the fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we've got time and we've got each other, and that I can carry the rent for a while if she needs to study. I'd tell my girlfriend Ana that I can carry the rent for a year if driving buses stops being a job.

say: I'd say **unions and councils** need to act now, not wait.
I'd share news about **retraining money** for neighbours losing office jobs.
think: About a **fifth of my week**, the paperwork, would move to software.
My real fear is **Ana's bus job** as driverless trials speed up.
do: Learn the **site software** properly instead of dodging it.
Join the **union** I keep putting off.
Price a **retraining plan** for Ana, such as depot engineering.
feel: **Uneasy**, with her eye on Ana more than her own work.
S1.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend Ana that I can carry the rent for a year if driving buses stops being a job.
fieldNote: Her own job looks **safe**, but the **household** risk sits with her partner.
She admits she's never joined the **union** despite her views.
She's ready to **carry the rent** for her partner, which shows where her loyalty sits.

steps.text: Learn the contractor's new site software in the first months
Join the construction union this year
Price a depot engineering course for Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political choice as much as a technical one, and I'd be loud about it. Online I'd be pushing for a guaranteed income or at least long, paid retraining. At work I'd tell the crew to get organised, because two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it hits our house twice. If AGI runs the planning by 2028, my foreman role gets thinner, and if robots can do refurb work by 2031, I'm thirty-two and out. Ana could go even sooner if driverless buses count as the thinking side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start putting 400 a month away, twice what we do now, and stop eating out. Push Ana to start a course straight away rather than wait. And I'd go to the union and the tenants' association both, because the people in those flats would lose their jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, for the first time in this conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots doing refurb work by 2031. Do you think old buildings would slow them down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. A new estate is easy for a robot, everything square and repeated. My flats are crooked and full of people's stuff, so I might get an extra year or two. Crooked sixties walls might buy me a year or two, but crooked walls are not a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. We'd sell it and get bus passes, which is a bit of a sad joke given Ana's job. That's about 200 a month we'd save straight away.

say: I'd call this a **political choice** and push for guaranteed income or paid retraining.
I'd tell the crew to **organise** now, since two years is nothing.
think: Both of us could lose work by **2031**, me at thirty-two.
Ana might go even sooner if **driverless buses** come with the thinking AI.
do: Save **400 a month** and stop eating out.
Sell the **car** and switch to bus passes to save 200 a month.
Work with the **union** and the tenants' association together.
feel: **Properly scared**, for the first time in the interview.
S2.quote: Crooked sixties walls might buy me a year or two, but crooked walls are not a retirement plan.
fieldNote: She expects **both earners** to lose work within five years, so she's alarmed.
Old, **crooked buildings** might buy her time, and she knows it isn't much.
She links her fate to the **tenants**, which is unusual and telling.

steps.text: Save 400 a month, double the current amount
Sell the car and switch to bus passes
Join forces with the union and the tenants' association
Campaign online for a guaranteed income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so use them: retraining money, a say for unions, not just a press release. I'd still be loud, but less shouty than with the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking AI and about eight for robots means I'm about thirty-five before the carpentry goes. That's long enough to make a real plan. Ana would have time too, if she starts early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get Ana into a depot engineering course in the first year, while I keep the money coming in. Learn every bit of site software I can, so I'm the one who runs the robots when they come. Save 250 a month on top of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which makes it bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one who runs the robots. Does that sit well with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not perfectly. I'd rather a union-trained foreman ran them than some kid from a tech company who's never fitted a door. If they're coming anyway, I want a seat at the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. My stair fitter Kemal is fifty-one, hates computers and is the best I've ever worked with, and no robot plan of mine saves him.

say: I'd say five years should mean **retraining money** and a union say.
I'd stay vocal but **less shouty** than in the fast picture.
think: My carpentry likely lasts until about **thirty-five**, time to plan.
Ana has **time to retrain** if she starts early.
do: Get Ana into a **depot engineering** course in year one.
Learn every bit of **site software** to be the one running robots.
feel: **Anxious**, but the plan makes it bearable.
S3.quote: My stair fitter Kemal is fifty-one, hates computers and is the best I've ever worked with, and no robot plan of mine saves him.
fieldNote: She'd rather a **union-trained foreman** ran the robots than a tech firm.
Her deepest worry is **Kemal**, her older stair fitter.
Five years turns her fear into a **household plan**.

steps.text: Enrol Ana in a depot engineering course this year
Learn every piece of site software the contractor uses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we don't. I'd be pushing the council to train refurb crews for the robot age, not just new-build crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about forty when robots could do my work. Ana could move into engineering at her own pace. Honestly, I think we'd be okay, as long as we don't fall asleep for nine years and wake up surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the job I love for a good few years. Ana does her course part-time while driving. I'd also start a part-time building surveying course in about year three, so I've got a second string by forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. Ten years is a long time in a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a surveying course. Why surveying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can already look at a wall and tell you what's wrong with it. A surveyor gets paid for that look. My eye for a crooked wall is the one thing I own that might still be worth money in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about getting married in a couple of years. With ten years, I'd say do it, have the party, and start saving for a deposit, not hide money under the bed.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** if used well.
I'd push the council to train **refurb crews** for robots, not only new-build crews.
think: I'd be about **forty** when robots could do my work.
We'll be fine if we don't **fall asleep** for nine years.
do: Keep doing the **refurb work** I love for several more years.
Support Ana through a **part-time course** while she keeps driving.
Start a part-time **surveying course** around year three.
S4.quote: My eye for a crooked wall is the one thing I own that might still be worth money in 2039.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her plan **calmly** and keep the wedding.
She turns her **eye for faults** into a career route.
Her **steady** adaptability shows: she moves, but not first.

steps.text: Keep running the refurb crew for several more years
Start a part-time building surveying course in year three
Go ahead with the wedding to Ana

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it could take both of our jobs inside five years. What would help is paid retraining that you can do while you still earn, and a union that has a real say in how robots come onto sites. Ana drives a bus and I fix crooked flats, and the fast picture could take both of our jobs before we've even married.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The tenants. Nobody asks what happens to an eighty-year-old woman when a robot turns up in her kitchen instead of me. I'd want someone to think about that.

headlineQuote: Ana drives a bus and I fix crooked flats, and the fast picture could take both of our jobs before we've even married.
portrait: **Olga** is a 27-year-old **carpentry foreman** refurbishing old social housing flats with tenants still living in them.
She lives with her girlfriend **Ana**, a bus driver, with about **three months** saved.
She uses AI tools **now and then** for snag lists and moves once others have tested things.
Her own job feels fairly safe, but **Ana's job** drives her worry in every picture.
She wants **unions, councils** and paid retraining to share the load.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Ana could **both** lose work within five years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that can be done while still earning.
A **union say** in how robots come onto sites, with thought for tenants.
